Family Health

Nipple changes outside breastfeeding: when to get checked

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Nipple symptoms can occur in women and men, whether or not they have ever breastfed. Irritation and benign duct changes are among the possible explanations, but a new symptom should not be diagnosed by its appearance alone. This guide focuses on changes outside breastfeeding and recent childbirth, with a separate note about the temporary breast changes that newborn babies can develop.

Notice the pattern, not just the colour

Nipple discharge may look milky, clear, yellow, green, brown, bloodstained or pus-like. Note whether it leaks without touching the breast, comes from one or both sides, or appears to come from one opening or several. Colour is useful information for the clinician, but it cannot reliably sort all benign and serious causes.

Other changes include soreness, itching, cracks, crusting, bleeding from the skin, swelling or a nipple that newly turns inward. Changes in the surrounding darker skin, called the areola, or dimpling elsewhere on the breast also deserve attention. A longstanding nipple shape is different from a recent change.

Breast tenderness can fluctuate with the menstrual cycle, and pregnancy can change breast sensitivity. Neither explanation should be assumed for persistent focal pain, a new lump or unexpected discharge. Avoid repeatedly squeezing the nipple to check: stimulation can encourage further discharge and make the pattern harder to assess.

When to arrange an assessment

Arrange a healthcare appointment for nipple discharge outside pregnancy or breastfeeding, including discharge from either nipple in a man. Many causes are not cancer, but assessment is still worthwhile. Tell the clinician if discharge is spontaneous, one-sided or bloody, or if there is a lump, new inversion or persistent nipple rash.

A painful, hot or swollen breast, especially with fever or feeling unwell, needs urgent assessment for infection or an abscess. Redness may be less obvious on darker skin, so warmth, swelling and pain also matter. Do not try to drain a swelling yourself.

A persistent one-sided scaly or crusted nipple can resemble eczema but occasionally has another cause, including Paget disease of the breast. Seek review if it does not improve with an agreed treatment plan. A temporary response to a cream does not replace follow-up if the change persists or returns.

Irritation, injury and infection

Rubbing from clothing during running or other exercise can make nipple skin sore or cracked. Contact with an irritating skin product, repeated stimulation, sexual activity or an injury to the chest can also contribute. The history helps distinguish a surface skin problem from fluid emerging from a milk duct; they are not always the same process.

For friction, adjust the fit and fabric of clothing and reduce the rubbing that provokes symptoms. A comfortable supportive sports bra or a suitable protective covering may help, depending on the person and activity. A very tight garment can add irritation rather than solve it. Stop a suspected fragranced product instead of adding multiple new creams.

Eczema may need a clinician-recommended moisturiser and anti-inflammatory treatment. A bacterial infection may require antibiotics; antifungal treatment is appropriate only when a fungal cause is supported. An abscess may need drainage as well as medication. These treatments are not interchangeable, and persistent symptoms need reassessment rather than repeated self-treatment.

Benign changes inside the milk ducts

Duct ectasia means ducts behind the nipple have widened and may collect fluid. It is a benign change that can cause discharge, tenderness or nipple inversion. It can affect one or both breasts and is more common as breasts age, although younger people can also develop it. A new inversion still needs checking before it is attributed to ectasia.

Once the diagnosis is established, many cases settle without treatment. Infection in the affected ducts may need antibiotics. Persistent troublesome discharge can sometimes lead to a discussion about removing an affected duct or ducts. That is an individual decision, not a requirement for everyone with the condition.

An intraductal papilloma is a small, noncancerous growth in a milk duct that can cause discharge, including bloodstained discharge. Calling a growth benign does not automatically mean no procedure or follow-up is needed. The team considers the biopsy result, any atypical cells, symptoms and whether the sample explains the imaging findings when recommending observation or removal. Ask how duct surgery could affect future breastfeeding.

Milky discharge, hormones and medicines

Milk-like discharge when someone is not breastfeeding is often called galactorrhoea. Pregnancy, nipple stimulation, some medicines, an underactive thyroid and raised prolactin are among the explanations clinicians may consider. A medicine and supplement review matters; do not stop a prescription on your own to see whether the discharge disappears.

Prolactin is a hormone involved in milk production. A prolactinoma is a usually noncancerous pituitary tumour that makes excess prolactin. A raised result does not by itself prove there is a tumour: medicines, other illnesses and temporary influences can affect the measurement. Changes in periods, sexual function, headaches or vision help guide assessment.

Treatment follows the cause. An underactive thyroid is generally treated with thyroid hormone replacement such as levothyroxine, with monitoring. For a confirmed prolactinoma, dopamine-agonist medicines such as cabergoline or bromocriptine can lower prolactin and shrink the tumour. Some small, minimally symptomatic findings may be monitored instead, depending on specialist assessment.

Vision symptoms need prompt specialist attention, but they do not automatically mean surgery is the only treatment. Surgery may be considered when medicines are unsuitable or ineffective, or for other individual reasons. Radiation is used much less often, generally in selected resistant cases. It is not the routine next step for everyone whose first medicine does not work.

What the appointment and tests may involve

Bring a short account of when the change began, whether it is spontaneous, and whether it follows exercise, menstrual changes or a new medicine. Mention pregnancy possibility, recent lactation, chest injury and skin products. A clinician may examine both breasts or the chest, nipples and nearby areas, explaining the examination and offering a chaperone according to your preferences and local practice.

Imaging depends on the type of discharge, age and examination. Ultrasound and diagnostic mammography can provide different information and are sometimes used together. Ultrasound is commonly the first test for concerning discharge in women under 30. Some physiologic discharge patterns do not require additional imaging once clinically assessed and routine screening is current.

A ductogram, also called galactography, is a specialised test in which a small amount of contrast is introduced into a discharging duct before X-ray images are taken. It may be useful in selected situations; it is not a routine test of every nipple’s function or a count of how many ducts are working.

A sample of abnormal skin may be needed for a persistent nipple lesion, and a needle biopsy may sample a finding within the breast. With milky discharge, pregnancy, prolactin and thyroid testing may be considered. Pituitary MRI is used when hormonal findings and the wider assessment warrant it; a brain CT or MRI is not automatic for every nipple symptom. Ask when results are expected and who will explain the next step.

If Paget disease of the breast is diagnosed

Paget disease is a rare breast cancer involving the nipple and usually the areola. Diagnosis requires assessment and typically a skin biopsy, with breast imaging to look for disease beneath the surface. The absence of a felt lump does not rule it out or establish how much disease is present.

Treatment depends on whether there is underlying ductal carcinoma in situ or invasive cancer, its extent and other tumour features. Some people can have breast-conserving surgery that removes the affected nipple and areola, usually with radiotherapy. Others need or choose mastectomy. Finding another tumour does not, by itself, make removal of the entire breast mandatory in every case.

The breast team also decides whether lymph-node assessment or treatments that act throughout the body are appropriate. The plan should explain the reason for the recommended surgery and alternatives. An article cannot choose an operation from the appearance of a rash or from one imaging result.

A separate note about newborn babies

Newborn girls and boys can have temporary breast swelling and a few drops of milk-like fluid because of hormone exposure around birth. This is different from an adult developing new discharge. It often settles over weeks, although swelling can last longer; there is no need to squeeze out the fluid.

Do not massage or squeeze a baby’s breast or nipple, because that can cause injury or infection. Contact the baby’s clinician if the area becomes red, hot, tender or increasingly swollen. Fever, poor feeding or a baby who seems unwell needs prompt medical assessment rather than reassurance based on the normal newborn explanation.

Make follow-up part of the plan

Reducing friction and avoiding an identified irritant can help prevent a recurrence of that particular skin problem. It cannot prevent every cause of discharge or every breast disease. Keep any review appointment, especially if symptoms were being observed rather than biopsied or treated.

If a test is reassuring but the symptom continues, ask whether the result explains the finding and what changes should bring you back sooner. Return for new spontaneous discharge, a new lump, worsening skin changes or persistent symptoms despite treatment. A useful plan gives you both an explanation and a clear next step.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

NHS and ACR/RSNA guidance support clinical assessment and selecting imaging by the discharge pattern and patient factors.

Independent breast, endocrine and dermatology references distinguish benign duct changes, hormone-related discharge and skin disease from conditions requiring biopsy or cancer treatment.

How BeMama can help

Record the change without repeatedly squeezing the nipple. Bring your medicine list and ask what each proposed test is intended to answer.

When to seek help

This article cannot diagnose discharge or a nipple rash. Arrange assessment for new discharge or persistent changes; painful warmth, swelling, fever or illness needs urgent care.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Discharge colour alone cannot establish the cause.
  • Persistent one-sided nipple changes, new inversion and unexpected discharge deserve assessment.
  • Treatments range from irritation care or monitoring to medicines and selected procedures, according to the diagnosis.
  • Temporary newborn breast swelling is a separate situation: never squeeze or massage it.

Frequently asked questions

Does green or milky discharge mean it is harmless?

Not by colour alone. Whether it is spontaneous, one-sided, associated with a lump or accompanied by other symptoms helps guide the assessment.

Should I squeeze the nipple to see if fluid is still there?

Avoid repeated checking by squeezing. It can encourage discharge or irritate the skin. Tell the clinician what you have already noticed.

Can a man develop nipple discharge?

Yes. It should be assessed rather than dismissed because the person has not breastfed.

Does every nipple symptom need a mammogram?

No. The examination, discharge pattern and age guide testing. Ultrasound, mammography, a biopsy or hormone tests answer different questions.

Does a benign papilloma always stay in place?

No. Monitoring or removal depends on symptoms, pathology, any atypia and whether the biopsy explains the imaging finding. Discuss the specific recommendation with the breast team.

Does a prolactinoma always require surgery?

No. Medicines often lower prolactin and shrink the tumour. Surgery and, more rarely, radiation are selected for particular circumstances.

Does Paget disease always mean mastectomy?

No. Some people are candidates for breast-conserving surgery with radiotherapy. The extent and type of any underlying cancer and individual preferences affect the plan.

Can newborn breast swelling produce milk?

Yes, temporary hormone-related swelling and a little milky fluid can occur in girls and boys. Do not squeeze it, and seek advice for redness, tenderness, fever or illness.

What if the symptoms continue after a normal test?

Return to the clinician and ask whether that test explains the symptom and what follow-up is needed. New or worsening changes should be assessed again.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
